variants.stem: Which plane divides the body vertically into anterior and posterior sections?
A cut that separates the body into a front half and a back half follows which plane?
Which body plane is also called the frontal plane?
Which plane runs vertically at right angles to the midline of the body?
An imaging view splits the body into a belly-side half and a back-side half. Which plane is it?
Which plane separates the anterior structures from the posterior structures?
Of the three primary body planes, which one passes from one side of the body to the other, dividing front from back?
The nose lies on one side of this plane and the back of the head lies on the other. Which plane is it?

questions.why: The coronal (frontal) plane divides the body vertically into front (anterior) and back (posterior) parts.
questions.deep: Sagittal = vertical, left/right sections (parallel to the midline). Coronal/frontal = vertical, front/back. Transverse/horizontal = upper (superior) and lower (inferior) halves. Memory aid: a Coronal plane is like the Crown-shaped headband that sits front to back; a sagittal cut is like an arrow flying straight ahead, splitting left from right.

variants.stem: Ovulation, the release of a secondary oocyte, is induced by a surge in which hormone?
Which hormone surge triggers the release of an egg from the ovary?
At about the midpoint of the ovarian cycle, a rapid rise in which pituitary hormone causes ovulation?
An ovulation test strip works by detecting a surge in which hormone?
Which anterior pituitary hormone prompts the mature follicle to rupture and release an oocyte?
After the follicular phase, which hormone peak induces ovulation and the formation of the corpus luteum?
FSH matures the follicle. Which different hormone then triggers ovulation?
Which hormone is responsible for the event that separates the follicular phase from the luteal phase?

questions.why: A surge in luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary induces ovulation, the release of a secondary oocyte from the ovary.
questions.deep: Ovarian cycle: follicular phase (FSH matures the follicle, which secretes estrogen) → ovulation (LH surge) → luteal phase (the corpus luteum secretes progesterone and estrogen). Memory aid: FSH = Follicle growth, LH = Launches the egg.

variants.stem: Which hormone released by an implanted blastocyst prevents the corpus luteum from degrading?
Home pregnancy tests detect which hormone?
Which hormone keeps the corpus luteum producing estrogen and progesterone in early pregnancy?
After implantation, the embryo signals the ovary to maintain the uterine lining by releasing which hormone?
Which hormone appears in the mother's blood and urine soon after a blastocyst implants?
Which hormone made by early embryonic tissue prevents the uterine lining from being shed?
Without which embryonic hormone would the corpus luteum regress soon after implantation?
Which hormone is the standard marker of early pregnancy?

questions.why: When a blastocyst implants, it releases hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum alive so it continues to secrete estrogen and progesterone.
questions.deep: By the second trimester the placenta makes enough estrogen and progesterone on its own, so hCG is no longer needed. Memory aid: hCG = Holds the Corpus luteum Going. Oxytocin is different: it stimulates uterine contractions and milk ejection.

variants.stem: Which neurotransmitter is released by motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction?
Skeletal muscle contraction is initiated when a motor neuron releases which chemical messenger?
Which chemical crosses the synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle fiber?
Which neurotransmitter binds receptors on the muscle cell membrane to trigger a muscle action potential?
Which neurotransmitter does the somatic nervous system mainly use to stimulate skeletal muscle?
A toxin blocks the receptors at the neuromuscular junction and causes muscle paralysis. Which neurotransmitter normally binds these receptors?
The axon terminal of a motor neuron releases which neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft of a muscle fiber?
Nerve signals reach skeletal muscle across a synapse. Which neurotransmitter carries that signal?

questions.why: Motor neurons release acetylcholine into the neuromuscular junction, where it binds receptors on the muscle fiber and starts contraction.
questions.deep: Sequence: action potential reaches the axon terminal → acetylcholine released → binds muscle receptors → muscle action potential → Ca²⁺ release → contraction. Memory aid: Acetylcholine = ACtion for muscle (Ach). Dopamine and serotonin act mainly in the brain.

variants.stem: In which organ do T lymphocytes mature?
Which lymphoid organ is located in the chest above the heart and is largest in childhood?
T cells are named for the organ where they mature. Which organ is it?
Which organ, located behind the sternum, trains developing immune cells to tell self from non-self?
Which organ shrinks with age and is the site of T-cell maturation?
Which structure is the maturation site for lymphocytes responsible for cell-mediated immunity?
Immature T cells travel from the bone marrow to which organ to complete their development?
Which organ would be most important for T-cell development in an infant?

questions.why: T lymphocytes begin in the bone marrow but mature in the thymus, which is why they are called T cells.
questions.deep: B cells mature in the bone marrow (B = Bone marrow); T cells mature in the Thymus. The thymus is a lymphoid organ behind the sternum that is most active in childhood and gradually shrinks (involutes) in adulthood.

variants.stem: Which tube carries urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder?
Urine leaves the renal pelvis through which structure?
Which structure connects each kidney to the bladder?
Peristalsis moves urine through which narrow muscular tubes toward the bladder?
Which structure transports urine from the kidneys to the bladder rather than from the bladder to the outside?
A kidney stone blocks the tube that drains urine from the kidney toward the bladder. Which structure is blocked?
Each kidney drains into a long, thin tube that leads to the bladder. What is this tube called?
Which part of the urinary system lies between the renal pelvis and the bladder?

questions.why: The ureters are a pair of muscular tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.
questions.deep: Urine pathway: kidney → ureter → bladder → urethra → outside. Memory aid: UreTER = kidney To bladder (two ureters, one for each kidney); UreTHRA = bladder to outside (one urethra).

variants.stem: Which organ absorbs water from remaining indigestible material and forms feces?
Which organ completes water absorption and compacts waste into feces?
Bacterial flora that help produce vitamin K live in which organ, which also forms feces?
Which organ includes the cecum, colon, and rectum?
Material that is not absorbed in the small intestine passes through the ileocecal valve into which organ?
Which part of the digestive tract stores feces until defecation?
The colon is the main part of which digestive organ?
Which organ is responsible for reabsorbing leftover water and electrolytes to produce solid waste?

questions.why: The large intestine (colon) absorbs remaining water and electrolytes from undigested material and compacts it into feces.
questions.deep: Large intestine parts: cecum → ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid colon → rectum → anus. Its bacterial flora ferment leftovers and make some vitamins (such as vitamin K). Most nutrient absorption already happened in the small intestine.

variants.stem: Which blood component adheres to exposed collagen and forms a plug when a vessel is damaged?
Which blood component is a cell fragment that helps start clotting?
Which blood components aggregate at an injury site to form a temporary plug before coagulation?
A person with a very low count of which blood component is most likely to bleed excessively?
Thrombocytes are another name for which blood component?
Which blood element releases chemicals that attract other cells and promote vasoconstriction at a wound?
Which blood component is involved in forming the initial clot at a site of bleeding?
Fragments of megakaryocytes circulate in the blood and are essential for hemostasis. What are they called?

questions.why: Platelets adhere to exposed collagen at a damaged vessel, release chemicals that attract more platelets, and form a plug that begins clotting.
questions.deep: Clotting steps: vessel constricts → platelet plug → coagulation cascade → prothrombin becomes thrombin → fibrinogen becomes fibrin mesh that traps platelets and red cells. Erythrocytes carry oxygen, leukocytes fight infection, plasma is the liquid portion of blood.

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which structures make up the central nervous system (CNS)?
Select all that apply: Which of the following are part of the CNS?
Select all that apply: Which of these belong to the peripheral nervous system (PNS), not the CNS?
Select all that apply: Which structures are part of the CNS?
Select all that apply: Which are components of the CNS?
Select all that apply: Which of these structures process and integrate information as part of the CNS?
Select all that apply: Which of the following are NOT part of the CNS?
Select all that apply: Which structures belong to the central nervous system?

questions.why: The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord, including all of their parts. Nerves and ganglia outside them make up the peripheral nervous system.
questions.deep: CNS = brain (cerebrum, cerebellum, diencephalon, brainstem) + spinal cord. PNS = cranial nerves, spinal nerves, and ganglia, which connect the CNS to the rest of the body. Memory aid: the CNS sits Inside bone (skull and vertebral column); the PNS reaches outside.

variants.stem: Tap the axon.
Tap the long fiber that carries impulses away from the cell body.
Tap the part of the neuron that conducts the action potential toward the axon terminals.
Tap the extension that transmits signals on to the next cell.
Tap the structure that ends in the axon terminals.
Tap the single long projection of the neuron, not the short branching ones.
Tap the part of the neuron that is often wrapped in a myelin sheath.
Tap the projection that leads away from the cell body toward other neurons or muscles.

questions.why: The axon is the single long projection that carries impulses away from the cell body toward the axon terminals.
questions.deep: Dendrites (the short, branching extensions) receive signals and carry them toward the cell body. The axon carries signals away. Memory aid: Axon = Away; Dendrites = Door-ways in. Many axons are wrapped in myelin, which speeds up conduction.

variants.stem: Which pancreatic hormone raises blood glucose by stimulating the liver to release stored glucose?
When blood sugar falls between meals, alpha cells of the pancreas release which hormone?
Which hormone triggers the breakdown of glycogen into glucose in the liver?
Which hormone is the counterpart that opposes the action of insulin?
After several hours without food, which pancreatic hormone rises to maintain blood glucose?
Which hormone increases blood sugar, in contrast to insulin, which lowers it?
Low blood glucose stimulates secretion of which pancreatic hormone?
Which hormone causes the liver to convert glycogen to glucose and release it into the blood?

questions.why: Glucagon, released by the pancreas when blood glucose is low, signals the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood.
questions.deep: Insulin lowers blood glucose by helping cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen; glucagon raises it. This is a negative feedback loop. Memory aid: GlucaGON = glucose GONE up (released into the blood); insulin lets glucose IN to cells.

variants.stem: Which type of RNA brings amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis?
Which molecule assists translation by matching its anticodon to an mRNA codon?
Found in the cytoplasm, which RNA delivers amino acids to the ribosome?
During translation, a ribosome follows mRNA instructions. Which RNA delivers the matching amino acids?
Which type of RNA contains an anticodon?
Which RNA molecule acts as the adapter between the genetic code and amino acids?
An amino acid attaches to one end of which type of RNA before reaching the ribosome?
Which RNA is the delivery vehicle of protein synthesis, bringing amino acids to the ribosome?

questions.why: Transfer RNA (tRNA) carries amino acids to the ribosome and matches them to mRNA codons through its anticodon during translation.
questions.deep: mRNA carries the DNA message from the nucleus to the cytoplasm; rRNA is part of the ribosome; tRNA is the amino acid carrier. Memory aid: tRNA = Transfer (delivers amino acids); mRNA = Message; rRNA = Ribosome.

variants.stem: In snapdragons, red (RR) is incompletely dominant over white (rr). What color are Rr plants?
A red snapdragon is crossed with a white snapdragon and neither allele is completely dominant. What color are all of the offspring?
When a heterozygote shows a blend of the two parental phenotypes, it is called incomplete dominance. In flowers with red and white alleles, what is the blended phenotype?
Under incomplete dominance, RR is red and rr is white. What is the phenotype of the heterozygote Rr?
Under incomplete dominance, which phenotype do heterozygous red/white flowers display?
A gardener crosses RR red flowers with rr white flowers. Under incomplete dominance, the F1 flowers will be:
Which color is expected when a flower inherits one red allele and one white allele and neither is completely dominant?
In incomplete dominance, the heterozygous phenotype is a mixture of the two homozygous phenotypes. If the homozygotes are red and white, the heterozygote is:

questions.why: In incomplete dominance neither allele is fully dominant, so the heterozygote (Rr) shows a blend of the two homozygous phenotypes: pink.
questions.deep: A cross of two pink snapdragons (Rr × Rr) gives 25% red, 50% pink, and 25% white, so the genotype ratio matches the phenotype ratio (1:2:1). Complete dominance hides the recessive allele in heterozygotes; incomplete dominance blends them.

variants.stem: What is the term for the passive movement of water across a cell membrane?
Water moves across a cell membrane through aquaporins without using ATP. This process is called:
Which process moves water across a membrane toward the side with the higher solute concentration?
Red blood cells placed in pure water swell because water enters them. Which process is responsible?
Which type of passive transport is specific to water?
Diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane is known as:
A plant cell loses water and wilts when placed in salt water. Which process moved the water out?
Which process requires no ATP, is driven by differences in solute concentration, and moves water?

questions.why: Osmosis is the passive transport of water across a selectively permeable membrane, driven by differences in solute concentration.
questions.deep: Passive transport (no ATP): simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion (uses channel or carrier proteins), and osmosis (water). Active transport uses ATP to move substances against their concentration gradient. Water moves toward the side with more solute.

variants.stem: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
In RNA, adenine pairs with which base?
Which base replaces thymine in RNA?
Which nitrogenous base is unique to RNA?
Which pyrimidine base appears in RNA but not in DNA?
During transcription, the DNA base adenine is paired with which RNA base?
Which base is absent in DNA but present in RNA?
RNA differs from DNA in having ribose and which base in place of thymine?

questions.why: RNA contains uracil (U) in place of the thymine (T) that DNA has, so uracil pairs with adenine in RNA.
questions.deep: DNA bases: A, T, G, C. RNA bases: A, U, G, C. RNA also uses ribose (not deoxyribose) and is usually single-stranded, while DNA is a double helix. Memory aid: U is for RNA's Unique base.

variants.stem: How many nucleotides make up a codon?
A codon on mRNA consists of how many nucleotides that together specify one amino acid?
Each amino acid is specified by a sequence of how many mRNA nucleotides?
The genetic code is read in groups of how many bases?
Which describes the length of a codon?
A start codon such as AUG contains how many bases?
A tRNA anticodon pairs with an mRNA codon. How many nucleotides are in each codon?
The sequences UUU, GGC, and AUG are examples of codons. Each contains how many nucleotides?

questions.why: A codon is a sequence of three nucleotides on mRNA that codes for one amino acid (or a start or stop signal).
questions.deep: With four RNA bases, three-base codons give 64 possible combinations, which is more than enough for the 20 amino acids. Several codons can code for the same amino acid. AUG is the start codon and also codes for methionine; UAA, UAG, and UGA are stop codons.

variants.stem: How does a catalyst speed up a chemical reaction?
opts: It is consumed in the reaction

variants.stem: Which statement about a catalyst is true?
opts: It is used up in the reaction

variants.stem: Enzymes are biological catalysts. What do they do to a reaction's activation energy?
What happens to the minimum energy needed for reactants to react when a catalyst is added?
Adding a catalyst lets more reactant molecules react because the catalyst:
A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction by affecting which quantity?
Which describes the role of a catalyst in a reaction mechanism?
opts: Lowers activation energy to speed the reaction
Raises activation energy to slow the reaction
Supplies extra energy as a reactant
Becomes part of the final product

variants.stem: A catalyst is added to a reaction. Which statement is true afterward?
opts: The reaction is faster and the catalyst is unchanged
The reaction is faster and the catalyst is used up
The reaction is slower and the catalyst is unchanged
The reaction is the same and the catalyst is used up

questions.why: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by lowering the activation energy, so more reactant molecules have enough energy to react. The catalyst itself is not consumed.
questions.deep: Other factors that increase reaction rate: higher reactant concentration, greater surface area, and higher temperature (more collisions with more energy). A catalyst does not change the products or make an impossible reaction occur; it only changes how fast the reaction reaches equilibrium.

variants.stem: Which type of attraction between water molecules gives water its cohesive and adhesive properties?
Water has a high specific heat because of which attraction between its molecules?
The slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule is attracted to the slightly negative oxygen of another. What is this attraction called?
Ice floats on liquid water because of which type of intermolecular attraction?
Which bond is weak, short-lived, and numerous, and helps hold water molecules together?
Which attraction is responsible for water's high heat of vaporization and also helps stabilize DNA?
Water can be pulled up a narrow tube against gravity because of cohesion. Which attraction causes this?
Which bond forms between a hydrogen atom and a highly electronegative atom such as oxygen or nitrogen on another molecule?

questions.why: Water molecules are polar, and the attraction between the slightly positive hydrogen of one molecule and the slightly negative oxygen of another is a hydrogen bond. These bonds give water its special properties.
questions.deep: Properties of water from hydrogen bonding: high specific heat, high heat of vaporization, cohesion and adhesion, good solvent for polar substances, and ice that floats. Hydrogen bonds are weaker than covalent and ionic bonds. They also hold the two strands of DNA together.

variants.stem: In a reversible reaction at equilibrium, more reactant is added. According to Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium will:
A + B ⇌ C + D is at equilibrium. If extra A is added, the system responds by:
Increasing the concentration of a reactant at equilibrium causes the system to:
Which response best describes how a system at equilibrium counters an added reactant?
opts: The net reaction proceeds toward products
The net reaction proceeds toward reactants
Both reaction rates drop to zero

variants.stem: The stress of adding more reactant to an equilibrium system is partly offset by:
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is at equilibrium. Adding more N₂ will cause the system to produce more of which substance?
A system at equilibrium is stressed by increasing a reactant's concentration. Which direction does it shift?
When the concentration of a reactant is raised in a closed equilibrium system, what happens?

questions.why: Le Chatelier's principle says a system at equilibrium responds to a stress by partly offsetting it. Adding reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right, toward the products.
questions.deep: Adding product shifts the reaction left; removing a reactant shifts it left; removing a product shifts it right. Heating an endothermic reaction shifts it right (heat acts like a reactant). Pressure only affects equilibria involving gases. A catalyst does not shift equilibrium.

variants.stem: What do elements in the same period (row) of the periodic table have in common?
opts: The same number of electron shells
The same number of valence electrons

variants.stem: Across a period, from left to right, which quantity stays the same?
Sodium, magnesium, and chlorine are in the same period. What do their atoms share?
opts: The same number of occupied electron shells
The same number of valence electrons

variants.stem: Which is true of all atoms in period 3 of the periodic table?
A horizontal row of the periodic table corresponds to which atomic feature?
Periods in the periodic table are organized by:
Moving down a column adds electron shells. Which statement describes elements in a single row?
opts: They have the same number of shells
They have the same number of valence electrons
They have the same atomic mass

variants.stem: Which feature does the period number tell you about an atom?

questions.why: Elements in the same period (horizontal row) have the same number of occupied electron shells, which equals the period number.
questions.deep: Groups (vertical columns) share the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties; periods (rows) share the same number of electron shells. Atomic number increases left to right across a period. Memory aid: Periods = Plateaus of shells (rows); Groups = Gangs with the same valence electrons (columns).

variants.stem: A solution has a hydrogen ion concentration of 1 × 10⁻⁴ M. What is its pH? Give a whole number.
Calculate the pH of a solution in which [H⁺] = 0.0001 M. Give a whole number.
The hydrogen ion concentration of a rainwater sample is 1 × 10⁻⁴ moles per liter. What is its pH? Give a whole number.
Using pH = −log[H⁺], find the pH when [H⁺] is 1 × 10⁻⁴ M. Give a whole number.
A solution contains 0.0001 mol of H⁺ per liter. What is the pH? Give a whole number.
Find the pH of a solution with a hydronium ion concentration of 1 × 10⁻⁴ M. Give a whole number.
A juice sample has [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁴ M. What pH does this give? Give a whole number.
If the hydrogen ion concentration of a solution is 10⁻⁴ M, what is the pH? Give a whole number.

questions.deep: For concentrations written as 1 × 10⁻ⁿ, the pH is simply n. Each pH unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration, and lower pH means more acidic. pH 4 is acidic; pH 7 is neutral; pH above 7 is basic.

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which of the following are subatomic particles that make up an atom?
Select all that apply: Which are particles found inside an atom?
Select all that apply: Which of these are located in the nucleus of an atom?
Select all that apply: Which particles carry an electrical charge?
Select all that apply: Which are the three basic pieces of an atom?
Select all that apply: Which particles contribute to an atom's mass number?
Select all that apply: Which of the following are NOT subatomic particles?
Select all that apply: Which of these exist outside the nucleus of an atom?

questions.why: Atoms are made of three subatomic particles: protons and neutrons in the nucleus, and electrons in shells outside it.
questions.deep: Protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral. Mass number = protons + neutrons (electrons have almost no mass). Atomic number = number of protons. Isotopes, ions, molecules, and compounds are things made from atoms, not particles inside them.

variants.stem: Convert 2.5 liters to milliliters.
A bottle holds 2.5 L of saline. How many milliliters is that?
A beaker contains 2.5 liters of solution. What is the volume in mL?
How many milliliters are in 2.5 L?
A lab technician measures 2.5 L of water. Express this volume in milliliters.
A reservoir tank holds 2.5 L of fluid. How many mL is this?
A solution volume of 2.5 L equals how many milliliters?
Using metric prefixes, convert 2.5 L to mL.

questions.why: The prefix milli- means one thousandth, so 1 L = 1000 mL and 2.5 L × 1000 = 2500 mL.
questions.deep: Common metric prefixes: kilo- (1000), hecto- (100), deka- (10), deci- (0.1), centi- (0.01), milli- (0.001), micro- (0.000001). To convert to a smaller unit, multiply; to a larger unit, divide. Moving the decimal 3 places right converts L to mL.

variants.stem: A researcher tests how different doses of caffeine affect reaction time on a computer test. Which is the independent variable?
opts: Time of day of the test

variants.stem: Participants receive 0, 50, or 100 mg of caffeine, and then their reaction times are measured. Which variable is deliberately changed by the researcher?
In a study of caffeine and reaction time, the researcher manipulates one variable. Which one?
A study compares reaction times after different caffeine doses. Which variable is the manipulated variable?
Which variable is the cause being tested when a study examines the effect of caffeine dose on reaction time?
A graph of reaction time versus caffeine dose is drawn. Which variable belongs on the x-axis?
In an experiment on caffeine and reaction time, which variable does the researcher choose and set before measurement begins?
Which of these would be labeled the independent variable in an investigation of how caffeine affects reaction time?

questions.why: The independent variable is the one the researcher deliberately changes. Here, the caffeine dose is changed to see its effect on reaction time.
questions.deep: Independent (manipulated) variable = what you change (x-axis). Dependent (responding) variable = what you observe and record (y-axis). Constants = everything else kept the same, such as age, time of day, and equipment. Only one variable should be changed at a time.

variants.stem: Which best describes a scientific hypothesis?
opts: A conclusion drawn after analyzing data
A summary of the final results
A fact that has been proven forever

variants.stem: Before running an experiment, a scientist writes a statement that can be tested and could be proven false. What is this statement?
Which is the proposed, testable answer to a scientific question, made before data are collected?
A student writes, "If plants get more sunlight, then they will grow taller." This statement is an example of a:
Which statement about a good hypothesis is true?
opts: It can be tested by experiment
It is proven true before testing
It is the same as a conclusion

variants.stem: Which step of the scientific method involves making a testable prediction about what will happen?
An educated, testable guess based on observation is known as a:
In the scientific method, what is formed after observing and asking a question but before experimenting?

questions.why: A hypothesis is a testable prediction or proposed explanation, written before the experiment, that data can support or refute.
questions.deep: Typical order: observation → question → hypothesis → experiment (with variables and controls) → data analysis → conclusion → communication of results. A hypothesis is not proven; it is supported or rejected by evidence. Good hypotheses are often written as If…then… statements.
